layers.frequency: counted from data/injuries.json — the official NFL injury reports for this pool
layers.recovery: from data/injury-curves.json, derived from those same reports
layers.research: from data/injury-research.json, the hand-written sourced layer — TWENTY injuries, each with a named study behind it. Everything else says it has none.

caveats: A body part on an injury report is what a team chose to declare. Teams are inconsistent about it, and a player placed on IR drops off the report entirely — so the counts here understate the season-ending cases rather than capturing them.
A named condition without a research entry is listed because it genuinely occurs at that region, NOT because we have data on it. The page says so rather than printing a timeline nobody can check.
Recovery figures are the median across this pool over three seasons, not a prognosis for any individual. Sample sizes are stated and several are small.

conditions.name: Concussion
conditions.note: Return is governed by a league protocol, not by how a player feels.

research.sources: Neurosurgery (2022), Harvard Football Players Health Study, OJSM
research.returnRateLabel: 89% return same season
research.reinjuryLabel: 5.3–8.3% same-season repeat risk after first concussion
research.performanceLabel: No significant acute performance decline in most studies
research.careerImpact: Players with 3+ concussions have elevated retirement risk. WRs 70% more likely to report long-term cognitive impairment (Harvard FPHS).
research.fantasyImpact: Minimal short-term fantasy impact. Long-term dynasty concern only if pattern develops (3+ career concussions). Monitor contested catch rate as a risk indicator.

research.sources: Spine and Axial Skeleton Injuries in the National Football League, AJSM (2012); Impact of Cervical and Lumbar Spine Surgeries on NFL Player Performance and Return-to-Play Outcomes, Cureus (2025); Return to Play Guidelines After Cervical Spine Injuries in American Football Athletes (2021)
research.returnRateLabel: 47% return after a CERVICAL spine procedure — materially worse than the lumbar equivalent
research.avgReturn: Usually short; the surgical path is not
research.reinjuryLabel: Stingers were the most common spine injury and raise the risk of a more severe re-injury
research.performanceLabel: Among those who returned after surgery, no significant change in performance
research.careerImpact: Cervical spine injury runs at about 0.42 per 1,000 exposures. The cervical spine is the one part of this map where the surgical outcome is genuinely worse than average.
research.fantasyImpact: Ordinary neck stiffness is nothing. The reason to read carefully is that the cervical spine is where the serious version lives — fewer than half return after cervical surgery, against three in five for the lower back.

conditions.name: Stinger / burner
conditions.note: A nerve injury, usually brief, and rarely reported as such.

research.sources: Epidemiology of Stingers in the National Football League 2015–2019 (2024); NFL Combine cervical spine injury history analysis; Brachial plexus injuries in the contact athlete: a narrative review, Annals of Joint
research.returnRateLabel: 76% of NFL players miss no time whatsoever
research.avgReturn: Most miss no time at all
research.reinjuryLabel: Recurrence is the norm rather than the exception in contact sport
research.performanceLabel: Not measured; single events resolve before the next snap
research.careerImpact: A single stinger is nothing. Repeat episodes correlate with cervical stenosis — smaller Torg ratio in players with multiple episodes (0.75 against 0.87) — and that is what ends careers.
research.fantasyImpact: Almost never worth acting on. Three in four cost no time. The reason to care is a player with a history of them, where the pattern rather than the episode is the story.

conditions.name: AC joint sprain
conditions.note: The most common shoulder injury in the league. Graded I to VI; the low grades play through it.

research.sources: Lynch et al, Acromioclavicular joint injuries in the National Football League: epidemiology and management, NFL Injury Surveillance System 2000–2011 (2013)
research.returnRateLabel: Over 98% treated without surgery and return
research.reinjuryLabel: Recurrence not separately reported
research.performanceLabel: No study has measured performance after AC injury specifically; other shoulder injuries show no measurable drop
research.careerImpact: Not career-altering. 96% of NFL cases are low-grade types I and II.
research.fantasyImpact: A shoulder separation sounds worse than it plays. It is the most common shoulder injury in the league and costs a game or two — except at quarterback, where the throwing shoulder roughly doubles the absence.

research.sources: Return to play following nonsurgical management of superior labrum anterior-posterior tears: a systematic review, JSES (2022); Dillon et al, Return to Play, Performance, and Career Longevity After Shoulder Labral Repair in the National Football League: A Matched Cohort Analysis, OJSM (2026)
research.returnRateLabel: Return rates across the literature span 20% to 94% — the widest range of any injury on this page
research.reinjuryLabel: Not separately reported
research.performanceLabel: 40% to 94% good or excellent results after arthroscopic repair
research.careerImpact: A concurrent rotator cuff tear carries a materially worse prognosis than the labral tear alone.
research.fantasyImpact: The honest answer is that nobody can tell you. Published return rates run from one in five to nine in ten, which means the label 'labrum' by itself predicts almost nothing — what it is torn WITH matters more than that it is torn.

research.sources: Return to play after rotator cuff tear in National Football League athletes — 29 athletes, mean age 27.4, JSES International (2023)
research.returnRateLabel: 79.3% of NFL players return at the same professional level
research.avgReturn: Varies with treatment; returning players averaged 2.8 more seasons
research.reinjuryLabel: Retear rate not separately reported in the NFL cohort
research.performanceLabel: Around 80% return at the same performance level regardless of how it was treated
research.careerImpact: Age decides it. Players over 30 were significantly less likely to return and are counselled accordingly.
research.fantasyImpact: Four in five come back at the same level — but the study's players averaged 27 at the time of injury. For anyone the wrong side of 30 this is a different, worse injury.

research.sources: Return to play after shoulder instability in National Football League athletes, Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery (2017)
research.returnRateLabel: 92% of NFL players return to regular-season play
research.avgReturn: Subluxation ~0 weeks; dislocation ~3 weeks; after surgery ~39 weeks
research.reinjuryLabel: 47% suffer a recurrent instability event — 26% after surgical repair against 55% without it
research.performanceLabel: Not separately measured in the NFL cohort
research.careerImpact: The first one rarely ends anything. The pattern of recurrence is what does.
research.fantasyImpact: He will probably not miss a game — and will probably do it again. Half of these recur, and a player who chooses surgery is gone for the season but far less likely to repeat it.

research.sources: Metacarpal Fractures in the National Football League: Injury Characteristics, Management, and Return to Play — 208 occurrences in 205 players, Journal of Hand Surgery (2022)
research.returnRateLabel: Nearly all return the same season
research.reinjuryLabel: Not separately reported
research.performanceLabel: Age, time in the league, position, mechanism and joint involvement showed NO relationship to time missed
research.careerImpact: Not career-altering.
research.fantasyImpact: One of the few injuries where position is not the whole story — the NFL study found no relationship between position and time missed. Under three weeks is the usual answer, and a skill player often plays through it in a cast.

conditions.name: Wrist sprain
conditions.noResearch: No NFL cohort study. Wrist injuries are usually reported under 'hand' and are rarely separated out.

research.sources: Gibbs D, Sahota S, Stevanovic O, et al. Elbow Dislocations in the National Football League: Epidemiology and Management. Cureus 13(11):e19241 (2021)
research.returnRateLabel: Not season-ending or career-ending in the NFL cohort
research.reinjuryLabel: Not separately reported
research.performanceLabel: Not separately measured
research.careerImpact: The study's conclusion in its own words: not a career-ending or season-ending injury.
research.fantasyImpact: Looks catastrophic on television and costs about a month. Nine in ten are managed without surgery at around 36 days; the one in sixteen that needs an operation runs closer to eleven weeks.

research.sources: Distal biceps ruptures in National Football League players: return to play and performance analysis — 35 players, JSES (2021); Characterization of distal biceps tendon and triceps tendon injuries in National Football League players from 2009 to 2022, Journal of Clinical Orthopaedics and Trauma (2025)
research.returnRateLabel: 33 of 35 NFL players (94%) returned after distal biceps repair
research.reinjuryLabel: Not separately reported
research.performanceLabel: Performance after surgery was similar to the same player before injury; no measured drop after either tendon
research.careerImpact: Career length does not appear to be affected, though offensive linemen played fewer games per season than controls.
research.fantasyImpact: Almost a full year out, and then he is himself again — one of the few severe injuries with no measured performance cost on return. Biceps skew defensive (73%) and triceps offensive (58%), so this rarely touches a fantasy roster.

conditions.name: Rib fracture or contusion
conditions.noResearch: No NFL cohort study. Rib injuries are managed case by case and rarely reach the literature.

conditions.name: Oblique strain
conditions.noResearch: No NFL cohort study. The published muscle-strain work covers the four big lower-body groups and stops there.

research.sources: Farooq et al, Surgically Treated Pectoralis Major Tears Impact the Play and Performance of NFL Athletes, Arthroscopy Sports Medicine & Rehabilitation (2022); Pectoralis Major Ruptures in the NFL: Incidence, RTP, and Performance Analysis, OJSM (2021)
research.returnRateLabel: 83–86% of NFL players return after surgical repair
research.reinjuryLabel: Re-rupture not separately reported in the NFL cohort
research.performanceLabel: A performance drop appears overall but disappears once players are matched for position and draft capital
research.careerImpact: Incidence has risen sharply — only 10 complete ruptures were recorded across 2000–2010.
research.fantasyImpact: A season, not a stretch. Ten months means an in-season tear is a full redshirt, and defensive linemen and receivers are the groups whose production has been shown to suffer on return.

research.sources: Spine and Axial Skeleton Injuries in the National Football League — 2,200+ injuries, 2000–2010, AJSM (2012); Impact of Cervical and Lumbar Spine Surgeries on NFL Player Performance and Return-to-Play Outcomes, Cureus (2025)
research.returnRateLabel: 61% return after a lumbar spine PROCEDURE — the vast majority never need one
research.avgReturn: Most are short; surgery is the exception
research.reinjuryLabel: Not separately reported
research.performanceLabel: Among players who returned after lumbar surgery, no significant change in performance
research.careerImpact: Spine injuries run to roughly 200 a season across the league, at about 0.93 per 1,000 exposures.
research.fantasyImpact: A back strain on the report is usually a week-to-week nuisance. It matters when the word changes — 'strain' and 'disc' are different injuries with different outlooks, and the surgical path returns only three in five.

research.sources: Hsu et al, The Professional Athlete Spine Initiative: outcomes after lumbar disc herniation in 342 elite professional athletes, The Spine Journal (2011); Statistical performance in NFL athletes after lumbar discectomy (2010)
research.returnRateLabel: 82% of NFL athletes return; 74% after lumbar discectomy
research.avgReturn: Non-operative often under a game; after discectomy, months
research.reinjuryLabel: Recurrence not separately reported
research.performanceLabel: No significant difference between pre- and post-operative performance score across the remaining career
research.careerImpact: Average career length after the injury is about 3.4 years. Surgically treated players had LONGER post-treatment careers than those managed without surgery.
research.fantasyImpact: Sounds career-threatening and usually is not — but it caps how long he has left rather than how good he is. Performance holds up; the remaining career is what shortens.

research.sources: Herzog et al, Lower Extremity Strains in the US National Football League 2015–2019, AJSM (2023); Orchard et al, Fifteen-week window for recurrent muscle strains, BJSM (2020)
research.returnRateLabel: Return rate not separately reported; nearly all return
research.avgReturn: Most return inside a week; a rectus femoris avulsion runs 6–12 weeks
research.reinjuryLabel: ~6% recur in the first match back, with risk elevated for 15 weeks after return
research.performanceLabel: Not separately measured
research.careerImpact: Rarely career-altering on its own; the pattern of repeat strains is the problem.
research.fantasyImpact: The second most common strain in the league after the hamstring — 21% of all time-loss lower-body strains. Usually a week, but the recurrence window runs three months, so a second one in the same season is normal rather than surprising.

conditions.name: Hip flexor strain
conditions.noResearch: No NFL cohort study. The league's strain research covers hamstring, adductor, quad and calf; the hip flexor is not broken out.

research.sources: Femoroacetabular Impingement in Professional Football Players: Return to Play and Predictors of Career Length After Hip Arthroscopy, Arthroscopy (2017); Hip Arthroscopy for Labral Tears and FAI in Professional American Football Athletes, Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine (2024)
research.returnRateLabel: 87% of professional football hip arthroscopies returned to play
research.avgReturn: Months after arthroscopy; not reported as a single figure for the NFL
research.reinjuryLabel: Revision rate not separately reported in the NFL cohort
research.performanceLabel: Return rates vary by position — linemen were significantly less likely to return
research.careerImpact: Position decides it. The same operation reads very differently for a lineman than for a skill player.
research.fantasyImpact: Rarely reported by name — it hides behind 'hip' on the injury report. High return rates for skill positions, but the surgery costs most of a season when it happens.

conditions.name: Hamstring strain
conditions.note: The most re-injured muscle in football. Coming back early is how one becomes three.

research.sources: Hamstring injuries in the National Football League: an epidemiological study, Journal of Clinical Orthopaedics and Trauma (2022); Jenkins et al, Risk and Prognosis of Hamstring Injuries in the National Football League: A 12-Year Review, OJSM (2024); Day et al, Correlation of Player and Imaging Characteristics With Severity and Missed Time in NFL Athletes With Hamstring Strain Injury, AJSM (2024)
research.returnRateLabel: ~95% return same season
research.reinjuryLabel: 38.4% recurrence rate in the NFL, and a 13.4% higher reinjury risk when a player returns inside two weeks — 23% of in-season recurrences land in the very first week back
research.performanceLabel: Minimal production impact once fully healed. Main risk is the re-aggravation cycle.
research.careerImpact: Not career-threatening on its own. Becomes a pattern concern when recurring — can lead to chronic management situations.
research.fantasyImpact: The most common soft-tissue injury that decides fantasy weeks: a third of NFL hamstring strains cost no games at all, and the mean for a non-recurrent one is 1.4. The trap is the quick return — coming back inside two weeks measurably raises the odds of doing it again, and a recurrence usually lands in the first week back.

research.sources: Herzog et al, Lower Extremity Strains in the US National Football League 2015–2019, AJSM (2023); Orchard et al, BJSM (2020)
research.returnRateLabel: Return rate not separately reported; nearly all return
research.avgReturn: Typically 1–3 weeks; a rectus femoris avulsion 6–12 weeks
research.reinjuryLabel: ~5% recur in the first match back, elevated for 15 weeks
research.performanceLabel: Not separately measured
research.careerImpact: Not career-altering.
research.fantasyImpact: The least common of the four big lower-body strains — 8% of the NFL's time-loss total — and the least likely to recur immediately. Usually a shorter absence than a hamstring of the same grade.

conditions.name: Thigh contusion
conditions.noResearch: No NFL cohort study. A deep thigh bruise is rarely reported separately from a quad strain.

conditions.name: ACL tear
conditions.note: The one that changes a career, not just a season.

research.sources: OJSM (2021), Arthroscopy Sports Medicine & Rehabilitation (2021)
research.returnRateLabel: 60–69% of WRs return
research.reinjuryLabel: ~25% re-tear risk (either knee) within 2-3 years
research.performanceLabel: Significant decrease in targets, receptions, yards, TDs vs. pre-injury
research.careerImpact: Career shortened by ~1.9 seasons vs. matched controls
research.fantasyImpact: Dynasty value typically drops 40-60% immediately. Year 1 back averages WR30-40 production. Year 2 bounce is real but inconsistent.

research.sources: Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries of the Knee at the National Football League Combine: An Imaging and Epidemiology Study — 69 of 2,285 combine players, AJSM (2018); Return to Play After Multiligament Knee Injuries in National Football League Athletes, Arthroscopy (2017); Evolving Treatment Patterns of NFL Players by Orthopaedic Team Physicians 2008–2016, OJSM (2018)
research.returnRateLabel: ~75% return to prior level
research.reinjuryLabel: Lower re-tear risk than ACL, but affects deceleration long-term
research.performanceLabel: Affects deceleration and cutting. Less devastating than ACL but still impactful for skill players.
research.careerImpact: Isolated PCL is survivable; combined is not the same injury. NFL players with ACL plus PCL or LCL involvement returned at 55.6%, and only 18.5% reached their prior level.
research.fantasyImpact: Dynasty discount of 20-30%. Most players return to near-prior production within one season. The key variable is whether other structures were also damaged.

conditions.name: MCL sprain
conditions.note: Graded I to III. The low grades are weeks, not months, and are often played through.

research.sources: Lundblad et al, UEFA Elite Club Injury Study — 130 MCL injuries of 4,364 registered, KSSTA (2019); Return to Play After Medial Collateral Ligament Injury (2016)
research.returnRateLabel: Nearly all return; isolated grade I–II are treated without surgery
research.avgReturn: Grade I ~13.5 days; Grade II–III ~29 days
research.reinjuryLabel: Recurrence not separately reported in the elite-football literature
research.performanceLabel: Low grades are frequently played through in a brace; no published NFL performance drop
research.careerImpact: Isolated MCL injury is not career-altering. Combined with an ACL tear it is, and the ACL drives that.
research.fantasyImpact: The knee injury you want. A grade I is often a one-to-two-game absence; a grade II runs three to five. Grade III, or any MCL alongside another ligament, is a different conversation entirely.

research.sources: Return to Play After Multiligament Knee Injuries in National Football League Athletes, Arthroscopy (2017)
research.returnRateLabel: 55.6% return when the LCL or PCL is torn ALONGSIDE the ACL
research.avgReturn: Isolated LCL is not separately reported in the NFL literature
research.reinjuryLabel: Not separately reported
research.performanceLabel: Only 18.5% of ACL-plus-PCL/LCL players regained their prior level, against 43.5% for ACL-plus-MCL
research.careerImpact: The lateral side is the bad side. An ACL with posterolateral corner involvement returns less often and less well than any other knee combination studied.
research.fantasyImpact: Almost never occurs alone, and what it occurs WITH is the whole story. An ACL tear with lateral-side involvement is a materially worse injury than the same ACL with an MCL — fewer than one in five got back to their prior level.

conditions.name: Meniscus tear
conditions.note: A trim and a repair are different operations with very different timelines.

research.sources: Systematic review of operative meniscal tears in elite athletes, JISAKOS (2021); Brophy et al, Meniscectomy and Resultant Articular Cartilage Lesions Among Prospective NFL Players, AJSM (2017)
research.returnRateLabel: 80–86% of elite athletes return after operative treatment
research.reinjuryLabel: Cartilage damage is the longer-term risk: 85% of NFL prospects with a prior meniscectomy had a chondral lesion on imaging
research.performanceLabel: Combine metrics were inferior in both the repair and meniscectomy groups
research.careerImpact: The operation matters more than the tear. A trim is weeks and costs meniscus you never get back; a repair is months and keeps it.
research.fantasyImpact: Ask which surgery. 'Meniscus' with a two-to-six-week timeline is a trim and he plays this season; a repair is a redshirt. American football was the most common sport in the elite-athlete literature.

research.sources: Acute Patellar Instability Injuries in the NFL: Who Gets Them, What Is the Treatment, and Outcome? An Analysis of Injuries From the NFL Database, 2000–2012 (ISAKOS); Return to Play Considerations After Patellar Instability (2022)
research.returnRateLabel: 81% managed without surgery and returning in under 40 days on average
research.avgReturn: Mean under 40 days when managed without surgery
research.reinjuryLabel: Recurrence not separately reported in the NFL cohort
research.performanceLabel: Not separately measured
research.careerImpact: Rare enough to be a curiosity: 54 cases in 13 NFL seasons, 0.17% of all injuries.
research.fantasyImpact: Rare, and rarer still at a skill position — it happens mostly to linemen blocking on pass plays. A subluxation is three times more common than a true dislocation and comes back faster.

research.sources: Herzog et al, Lower Extremity Strains in the US National Football League 2015–2019, AJSM (2023); Orchard et al, BJSM (2020)
research.returnRateLabel: Return rate not separately reported; nearly all return
research.reinjuryLabel: ~2% recur in the first match back — the lowest immediate recurrence of the major strains
research.performanceLabel: Not separately measured
research.careerImpact: Not career-altering, though it skews to older players.
research.fantasyImpact: 12% of the league's time-loss lower-body strains and the least likely to recur straight away. The worry is the Achilles above it — a calf complaint in an older player is worth watching rather than ignoring.

conditions.name: Shin splints
conditions.noResearch: No NFL cohort study. It is a chronic overuse complaint, so it rarely produces the discrete absence these studies count.

conditions.name: High ankle sprain
conditions.note: Different injury from a rolled ankle, and several times the absence.

research.sources: Return to Play After Isolated Syndesmotic Ligamentous Injury in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis, OJSM (2022); Corticosteroid Injections Hasten Return to Play of NFL Players Following Stable Ankle Syndesmosis Sprains, OJSM (2015); Miller et al, comparative time-loss for syndesmotic vs lateral ankle sprains in professional football
research.returnRateLabel: ~92% return same season
research.reinjuryLabel: ~15% same-season recurrence
research.performanceLabel: Significant impact on WR route-running and RB cutting ability. Residual effects 2-4 weeks after return.
research.careerImpact: Not career-threatening. But WRs playing through high ankle sprains show measurably decreased separation and burst metrics.
research.fantasyImpact: Expect 3-6 weeks missed. When player returns, discount production ~20% for 2-3 weeks. High ankle sprains are more impactful than low ankle sprains for skill players.

research.sources: Epidemiology and Outcomes of Ankle Injuries in the National Football League, OJSM (2022); Miller et al, comparative time-loss for syndesmotic vs lateral ankle sprains in professional football
research.returnRateLabel: 91% of all NFL ankle injuries return to play
research.reinjuryLabel: Up to 70% develop some chronic instability after recurrent sprains
research.performanceLabel: Little measured short-term effect; the risk is accumulation, not the single event
research.careerImpact: One is nothing. Recurrent instability is what eventually forces retirements, despite an initial return.
research.fantasyImpact: The most over-panicked injury on the report. A rolled ankle costs a fraction of a game on average — roughly a quarter of what a high ankle sprain costs. Check which one it is before you sell.

conditions.name: Achilles tear
conditions.note: Technically the heel, but it presents and is reported at the ankle.

research.sources: Return to Play Following Achilles Tendon Rupture in NFL Players Based on Position, Foot & Ankle International (2021); Epidemiology and outcomes of Achilles tendon ruptures in the National Football League, Orthopedics (2010); Career Outlook and Performance of Professional Athletes After Achilles Tendon Rupture: A Systematic Review, Foot & Ankle International (2021); Impact of Achilles tendon rupture on performance and career outcomes in NFL players: a matched cohort study, The Physician and Sportsmedicine (2026)
research.returnRateLabel: Only 38% of WRs return (lowest of all positions)
research.reinjuryLabel: ~12% re-rupture risk within 2 years
research.performanceLabel: Power rating down 22% and approximate value down 23% across the three years after return — a decline beyond ordinary aging
research.careerImpact: 26% never play in the NFL again. Return rate varies sharply by position: tight ends 71%, receivers 38%. Returning is not the same as recovering.
research.fantasyImpact: The most brutal injury on this page for a skill player. Even the ones who come back are measurably worse for three years, and running backs have shown the steepest fall of any position. Treat a return-to-play headline as the start of the story rather than the end of it.

conditions.name: Turf toe
conditions.note: Sounds minor and is not — the grade-3 version ends seasons.

research.sources: The Effect of Turf Toe Injuries on Player Performance in the National Football League, Foot & Ankle International (2020); Smith & Waldrop, Operative Outcomes of Grade 3 Turf Toe Injuries in Competitive Football Players, Foot & Ankle International (2018); Return to Play Following High-Grade Turf Toe Injuries in NFL Athletes, Orthopaedic Journal at Harvard Medical School (2021)
research.returnRateLabel: ~80% return, but often with lingering issues
research.reinjuryLabel: ~20% chance of chronic issues requiring additional procedures
research.performanceLabel: Affects push-off and acceleration. QBs lose mobility, WRs lose burst off the line.
research.careerImpact: Grade 3 (complete plantar plate tear) is significantly worse than Grade 1-2. Can become a chronic issue if not managed properly.
research.fantasyImpact: Expect 8-16 weeks missed. QBs often play through but with reduced mobility. Dynasty impact moderate — usually not career-ending but can linger for years.

research.sources: Abed et al, Return to Play, Performance, and Economic Analysis of National Football League Players After Lisfranc Injury, OJSM (2023); Performance-Based Outcomes Following Lisfranc Injury Among Professional American Football and Rugby Athletes (2018)
research.returnRateLabel: 81.8–83% of NFL players return to play
research.reinjuryLabel: Recurrence not separately reported
research.performanceLabel: Statistically significant fall in Approximate Value in the return year; offensive players decline more than defensive
research.careerImpact: Most return, but the year they come back is measurably worse than the year before.
research.fantasyImpact: Season-ending, and the following season is not a clean slate — the measured decline lands in the return year. Running backs and offensive linemen account for the largest share of these.

conditions.name: Plantar fasciitis
conditions.noResearch: No NFL cohort study — only individual player reports. Timelines in the press range from no games missed to two months, which is why none is stated here.

research.sources: Return to Play and Fracture Union after Surgical Management of Jones Fracture in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis — 646 fractures, JCM (2022); Optimal Time to Return to Play and Performance after Jones Fracture Surgery in the National Football League, OJSM (2017); Jones Fractures Identified at the NFL Scouting Combine, OJSM (2018)
research.returnRateLabel: 98.4% return across 646 fractures; 98.8% with intramedullary screw fixation
research.reinjuryLabel: Refracture runs 4–12%, and incomplete healing anywhere from 7% to 50%
research.performanceLabel: NFL players returning in UNDER 10 weeks had a significantly greater fall in performance than those who waited longer
research.careerImpact: Nonunion was found in 12.2% of combine cases. A refracture costs about 15 weeks.
research.fantasyImpact: The rare injury where rushing back is measurably punished — players who returned inside ten weeks performed significantly worse than those who did not. If the team is being cautious with a Jones fracture, that is the evidence-based choice rather than an abundance of caution.
